seo.meta_description: Toyota HiAce 1989-2004 / 2004-present import NZ. Compare H100 and H200 models, petrol and diesel options, grades, and what to confirm before bidding.
seo.og_description: Looking at a Toyota HiAce import from Japan? We help NZ buyers compare H100 and H200 vans, wagons and grades, then check availability, viability and auction details before bidding.

blocks.hero_subtitle: This is one of the easier vans for NZ buyers to understand because the HiAce has been used here for everything from courier work to shuttle duty. What matters is not the badge on its own, it is whether the exact auction car is H100 or H200, van or wagon, and which engine and seating layout it has. That exact-vehicle check also matters for import viability and compliance planning before bidding.
proof_points: Japan specialists with direct auction access
Importing estimate provided before bidding, with compliance as part of the process
blocks.why_kiwis_buy: People look at the HiAce because it uses its footprint well and there is a wide spread of body styles, from simple DX load vans through to passenger-focused wagon versions. For business use, that means you can search for a basic work van or a better-trim Super GL without changing model family. For family, shuttle or recreation use, the wagon and commuter side of the range opens up more seating, but that exact layout needs to be confirmed on each vehicle. That helps buyers avoid paying for the wrong configuration and gives a clearer view of whether the vehicle suits daily use and likely operating costs.
blocks.video_caption: A walkaround works best on a HiAce because you can see straight away whether it is set up as a cargo van, passenger wagon or something already modified. On this model, the side-door layout and rear cabin tell you a lot before you even get to the auction list.
blocks.main_usp_deep: The HiAce's main strength is range depth. The H100 covers older, simpler vans and wagons from 1989 to 2004, while the H200 from August 2004 onward gives you the shape most NZ buyers recognise, with petrol and diesel options and grades from DX to Super GL Dark Prime II seen in current listings. If you want the later 2.8-litre diesel, the 1GD-FTV is the same GD-family engine used in other Toyota commercial and 4WD models. Exact gearbox and drive layout still need to be confirmed on the listing, because HiAce specification varies more than many buyers expect.

buyer_persona.headline: Who is this car right for?
buyer_persona.body: This one suits buyers who need space first and image second, tradies, delivery operators, shuttle users, camper planners, or anyone who wants one model with a lot of body and trim choice. It also works for buyers who are happy to compare several auction cars carefully rather than assuming every HiAce is the same. If you want a practical daily vehicle with flexible load or seating options, it is a solid match.

car_specs_benefits.benefit: This is the long-running HiAce shape most NZ buyers know, which makes it easier to target familiar layouts and later diesel options.

car_specs_benefits.benefit: Shows why older H100 searches need careful engine-code checking, because the range spans simple petrol and diesel options across different use cases.
Useful for passenger or mixed-use buyers who want a naturally aspirated petrol option with straightforward power delivery.

car_specs_benefits.benefit: That 450 Nm matters in a van because it gives easier pulling power with passengers, tools or cargo on board.

car_specs_benefits.benefit: Lets buyers match the van to the job, simpler rear-drive for normal road use or 4WD where access and traction matter more.

standout_features_block.headline: What sets it apart
standout_features_block.intro: On a HiAce, the useful differences are in body layout, seating and trim rather than flashy gadgets.

items.title: Van, wagon and commuter body choices
items.body: The HiAce family covers cargo vans, passenger wagons and higher-seat commuter-style layouts across the H100 and H200 years. That matters because you can search one model line for very different jobs, from tools and freight to airport runs or group transport. The exact seating count and window layout need to be confirmed on the auction car.
items.image_hint: Side-on photo showing the full body profile and window layout so buyers can see whether it is cargo-focused or passenger-focused

items.title: DX to Super GL grade spread
items.body: DX is the simple end of the range for buyers who just want load space and fewer trim extras. Super GL and special editions such as Dark Prime II sit further up, aimed at buyers who want a more finished cabin and a less bare commercial feel. That grade ladder is one reason the HiAce works for both business and private use.
items.image_hint: Front cabin shot showing the dashboard, seat trim and storage layout of a higher-grade HiAce

items.title: Passenger-oriented Wagon GL option
items.body: The Wagon GL sits on the passenger side of the HiAce family and uses the 2.7-litre 2TR-FE petrol engine. It is worth knowing about because some buyers start by searching vans, then realise a wagon suits shuttle or family carrying better. It changes the whole brief from cargo-first to people-first.
items.image_hint: Rear cabin photo with multiple passenger seats visible to show the difference from a cargo van

items.title: Wide variation in fit-out
items.body: HiAce listings can include standard vans, passenger versions and already modified examples such as camper or accessibility conversions. That is useful if you want something purpose-built, but it also means the photos and auction list matter more than the badge. Two HiAces of the same year can be set up very differently.
items.image_hint: Rear cargo or rear cabin scene showing shelving, trim panels or conversion hardware that changes how the vehicle can be used

tech_deep_dive_block.headline: Under the skin
tech_deep_dive_block.intro: The important engineering story with a HiAce is generation, engine family and drivetrain layout.

items.title: H100 and H200 generations
items.body: The H100 ran from August 1989 to August 2004, covering van, wagon and commuter variants, with update points referenced in 1993, 1997 and 2002. The H200 replaced it from August 2004 and continues in Japan, which is why current import searches still centre on that platform rather than the overseas H300. For NZ buyers, that matters because the H200 is the familiar modern HiAce shape with a long production run. If you are comparing a 2004 vehicle, checking whether it is late H100 or early H200 is one of the first things to sort out.

items.title: H200 diesel engine families
items.body: H200 diesel options in the supplied model data include the 2KD-FTV 2.5, 1KD-FTV 3.0 and later 1GD-FTV 2.8. The 1GD-FTV is the standout later diesel in this range, with 177 PS and 450 Nm in Toyota's standard 2.8-litre tune. In plain terms, that is the sort of torque figure that suits a loaded van far better than a peaky engine would. Exact output, gearbox and grade pairing still need to be checked on the individual vehicle before bidding.

items.title: Rear-wheel drive and part-time 4WD layouts
items.body: H200 models were offered as rear-wheel drive or part-time 4WD depending on variant. Rear-wheel drive suits the basic van brief well because it keeps the layout simple and familiar for road use. Part-time 4WD is worth looking for if the van will be used where traction matters more, but it is not something to assume from the model name alone. The listing needs to confirm the drive layout, because it affects suitability.

items.title: Grade ladder and best-trim call
items.body: Current model data supports a simple ladder of DX at the basic commercial end, Super GL higher up the van range, and Super GL Dark Prime II as the standout premium van grade seen in current Japanese listings. On the passenger side, Wagon GL is the confirmed 2.7-litre petrol people-carrying option. If you want the best all-round van brief, Super GL Dark Prime II is the trim to watch, while DX still makes sense for buyers prioritising simple load-carrying specification.

models_comparison.intro: The HiAce range is broad enough that the real comparison is between generations and grades before you even compare it with another model.

rows.notes: Checked for the exact model code and vehicle before bidding; final certification occurs in NZ.
H100 includes older petrol and diesel engines such as 1RZ, 2RZ-E and 3L. H200 adds 1TR-FE 2.0 petrol, 2TR-FE 2.7 petrol, 2KD-FTV 2.5 diesel, 1KD-FTV 3.0 diesel and later 1GD-FTV 2.8 diesel.

DX is the basic commercial grade, Super GL sits higher for buyers wanting a more finished cabin, Dark Prime II is a recognised special-edition Super GL variant, and Wagon GL is the passenger-oriented petrol wagon grade confirmed in model data.
There is a wide spread of HiAce body styles and uses, so the better approach is to search by generation, roof, seating and engine rather than by badge alone.

faq_block.q: Can you source both H100 and H200 HiAce models?
faq_block.a: Yes, provided suitable vehicles are showing in current Japanese auction supply. The first step is telling us which generation, body style and use case you want, because HiAce covers a lot of different configurations.

faq_block.q: What costs make up a HiAce import?
faq_block.a: We prepare an importing estimate for the exact vehicle before bidding. The total depends on the vehicle, auction result and the work needed after arrival.

faq_block.q: Can you tell me if a HiAce is typically within the entry requirements before I bid?
faq_block.a: Import viability must be checked for the exact model code and vehicle before bidding. Final entry certification and compliance are completed in New Zealand after arrival and assessment.

faq_block.q: How long does the process take?
faq_block.a: Timing depends on when the right vehicle appears, whether your bid is successful, and shipping schedules after purchase. We keep you updated through the process rather than guessing dates too early.

faq_block.q: What do you provide from the auction side?
faq_block.a: We translate the auction list and explain the recorded grade, mileage, damage markings, condition notes and listed modifications where those details are present. Photos and supporting records vary between listings, so we tell you what is confirmed and what is not.

not_for_you_block.headline: Who this may not suit
items: Buyers who want one fixed specification without checking body style, seating and trim on each vehicle.
Anyone expecting every HiAce to be a simple cargo van, because wagon, commuter and modified examples can be very different.
People who only want the newest global-shape HiAce, because the Japanese line continues with the H200 family.

alternatives_block.intro: If the HiAce is on your list, these are the closest alternatives worth weighing up from the same import search.

rows.better_if: You want a direct rival in the same full-size van class and are happy to compare whichever model has the better auction options at the time.
rows.tradeoff: Grade and engine mix differ, so the best choice can come down to the exact vehicles available rather than a simple model preference.

rows.better_if: You need a people mover first and want a more passenger-focused cabin than a commercial van layout.
rows.tradeoff: It gives away cargo practicality and is not the same heavy-duty work tool as a HiAce van.

rows.better_if: You want a smaller people mover for family or shuttle use and do not need full-size van space.
rows.tradeoff: It has less load area and less commercial focus than a HiAce.

engine_drivetrain_block.headline: Powertrain options to consider
engine_drivetrain_block.body: For H100, confirmed model-level engines include older petrol units such as 1RZ and 2RZ-E, plus the 3L 2.8 diesel on some variants. For H200, confirmed engines include 1TR-FE 2.0 petrol, 2TR-FE 2.7 petrol, 2KD-FTV 2.5 diesel, 1KD-FTV 3.0 diesel and later 1GD-FTV 2.8 diesel. A current NZ HiAce using the 1GD-FTV is paired with a 6-speed automatic, but exact transmission on an imported auction vehicle still needs to be confirmed from that listing.

Confirm whether the vehicle is standard or modified
